section.title: Philip Su: Meta Levels, Management vs IC, and Choosing Your Career Goal
section.deck: Philip Su, a former Microsoft, Facebook and OpenAI engineer, reflects on rapid promotion, moving between management and individual contributor tracks, how senior levels are judged, and why wanting the right goal matters more than reaching it fast.

blocks.text: Philip Su is introduced by the host as one of the few engineers promoted to distinguished engineer (IC9) at Meta. Philip's view is that fast career growth rests on luck, talent and hard work, and that hard work buys speed at a real cost to health and relationships. The larger lesson Philip draws from a career at Microsoft, Facebook, a Gates-funded nonprofit and OpenAI is to decide what you actually want before sprinting toward it. The conversation covers moving between management and individual contributor tracks, a deliberate drop from E9 to E7, how seniority levels are judged, building Facebook's London engineering site, why Philip left Facebook and later joined OpenAI, how Philip learned to write, and whether to specialize or stay a generalist. Levels, headcounts and company history are Philip's recollections, and Philip flags several as dated.
blocks.heading: Philip Su's view: grow fast if you must, but choose the goal on purpose

blocks.question: What does Philip credit for the fast climb through Microsoft's ladder?
answer: Philip names several causes. One was working with very good managers and teammates. The Microsoft tablet PC team had about 20 people, and three of them were distinguished engineers, which Philip calls very rare at Microsoft. Philip learned a great deal quickly from them.

Another cause was very long hours. In the first year Philip kept a sleeping bag in the office and often slept there. Philip set a 3 a.m. alarm to follow what Philip describes as Da Vinci's idea of sleeping in two four-hour blocks, coding between them.

Philip sums up fast growth as luck, talent and hard work. Luck means being in the right place at the right time, for example being at Stanford when Sergey and Larry were there. Talent matters because Philip rejects the idea that anyone can become anything: Philip will never be a great basketball player, and a weak public speaker can become passable but not a Cicero. Hard work matters because someone who outworks equally talented and equally lucky people will get further. Philip adds that Philip does not recommend this to everyone.

followups.question: If the goal is growth at all costs, were those hours actually optimal?
answer: Philip says the work week is often defended by pointing to Henry Ford's finding that each added hour is less productive. Philip agrees that output per hour falls as one stays up too long, but says that for many people the curve runs a long way before an added hour becomes negative. In Philip's view, working 50 or 60 hours probably gets more done in total, though each extra hour is less effective.

Philip adds a second consideration with a surgeon analogy. Philip heard from a surgeon that the quickest way to gain surgical experience is to log many surgery hours, so a long residency may pack six years of exposure into four. Nobody wants a surgeon in the 34th hour, Philip says, but a surgeon with wide experience is valuable. Philip would not recommend the crazy hours Philip worked early on, yet they gave Philip far more experience than a typical junior Microsoft hire. There are diminishing returns, but still returns, so a person who truly puts career above all, including relationships, should work more. Philip says Philip's own work life was out of balance for years.
followups.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.question: Why did Philip become a manager, and why did the role keep changing?
answer: Philip says the promotion to the Microsoft equivalent of E7 came as a manager, after which Philip also worked as an individual contributor at that level. Early on Philip was very ambitious and came from a culture, as an ethnically Chinese person, in which managers were more respected and advanced further. Philip now calls the belief that management was the next growth step somewhat misguided.

Over a career Philip has moved between managing and individual contribution at least six times. Philip loves being an individual contributor but is often asked to manage, for example as a temporary manager.

followups.question: Did Philip step in on poorly managed teams, or did managers ask Philip for help?
answer: Philip says both happened. Philip's order of preference is individual contributor first, then manager of a team that lacks a better manager, and left to their own devices Philip would rather not manage people. Philip would rather manage a team that is poorly managed than leave it that way.
Philip also says that four separate times a former manager of Philip's asked to report to Philip.
followups.speaker: Philip Su

followups.question: How does a manager come to report to someone they used to manage under?
answer: Philip says each case differed. Sometimes the manager reported to Philip on the same team. Sometimes the manager asked, years later, to join Philip's team after both had moved on. In one same-team case the manager wanted to become an individual contributor while Philip, a strong individual contributor, wanted to manage, so it was almost a swap in place. In most cases Philip joined a team elsewhere and a former manager who liked working with Philip was happy to work for Philip there.

Philip suggests part of the reason is having learned from great managers. After chasing management early in the career, Philip stopped looking for management roles as actively as for individual contributor ones.
followups.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.question: How should someone decide between staying an individual contributor and becoming a manager?
answer: Philip is open to new experiences and generally advocates trying management if you think you might like it or be good at it, with a few caveats.

The first caveat is not to walk through a one-way door by accident. Philip has gone back to being an individual contributor roughly six times, but says many people cannot. They become managers of managers, drift far from the code, and are then unwilling to take a lower-level job or unable to meet an individual contributor's expectations at their old level. Philip kept the door open both ways by diving into code even while managing teams.

The second caveat is that people tend to think only about themselves when they want to manage. Philip's test is that you are ready to lead when your team would have elected you: "Would you want to work for you?" If the answer is not a solid yes, there is something to improve. Philip notes that nobody can truly make you lead, because teams can slow-roll or sandbag work, so people have to want to work for you. Philip expects that once those improvements are made, people will ask you to manage.
blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.question: Did Philip lose progress by switching between the two tracks?
answer: Philip says yes, intentionally and willingly. When Philip moved from site director of Facebook London to an individual contributor on Oculus, Philip was eventually releveled from E9 to E7. Philip bought into that and says it was necessary, because the skills shown as a site director differed from those needed to be a good coder on Oculus.

Many people cannot accept such a step, Philip says, either for ego reasons or because lifestyles grow to fill whatever compensation people earn. Those who will not change their lifestyle paint themselves into a corner with fewer and fewer jobs they can take.

Philip also says timing matters. One or two years into a career, a lateral move such as junior software developer to junior product manager is easy, and many people will coach you. Around the senior E5 range, moving from E5 software developer to E5 product manager is very difficult, unless the engineering work already involved product management. At more senior levels the skills converge again, so the shape is a diamond. An effective E8 individual contributor, in Philip's description, has a technical vision, understands infrastructure weak points, plans staged migrations, coaches well and understands business strategy. Philip concludes that the middle of a career is where changing tracks is hardest.

followups.question: Does the diamond come back for deep specialists, for example in AI?
answer: Philip agrees that for some archetypes it does not come back. Someone who goes very deep, for instance on SQL query optimization, may not need to develop the other skills that go with leading teams, and may not transition well into management.
followups.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.question: How did Philip handle the move down from E9 to E7?
answer: Philip had worried about this when first promoted from E8 to E9 as London site director. Philip told the Facebook CTO of the day (captioned "Shrep") that, because Philip liked being an individual contributor, Philip doubted the performance level could be kept when moving back to coding. The CTO replied that they should worry when it happened and not withhold a promotion because of a possible future return to coding.

Back in code, Philip understood the E9 expectations were out of reach. Being moved back to E7, the level Philip joined at about eight years earlier, felt great. Philip says it is far better to perform well at a level than to barely tread water at one where you feel imposter syndrome and doubt you will stay qualified. Philip also did not want pay above what Philip deserved relative to teammates.

Philip says few people make so large a change, and it demands a particular ego. Philip went from running a site of perhaps 400 or 500 people to reporting to a manager who reported to a manager. Philip also had to avoid voicing opinions about running the site, and avoid using outsized influence from the past, so the new leaders could succeed.
blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.question: What do engineers at E7, E8 and E9 typically do?
answer: Philip caveats that Philip's information is coarse and probably stale, since it comes from working at Meta starting about 15 years earlier. In general, levels reflect scope of influence: how big, long or valuable a project one can single-handedly guarantee. An intern might guarantee a small feature. A senior developer at E5 or E6 should deliver the work of about 10 to 15 people. At E7, Philip would expect regular influence over about 50 people, driving technical direction for a team that size, being consulted by product and engineering managers, and personally delivering about six months of work with no check-ins. A director might influence about a hundred people.

On the individual contributor side, Philip says large scope comes in different forms. Some people are narrow but deep in a way others cannot match, and four E6s cannot replace them. Others are broad generalists, especially valuable for new teams and startups, where three E6s cannot outperform one great generalist E8.

Philip stresses that the qualitative difference matters most and cannot be captured in an HR bullet list. People at those levels excel for different reasons, and someone more senior must judge them. When Philip was first promoted to E8, E9 did not exist. Philip says the company later had to invent such levels for individual contributors like John Carmack. Philip recalls, if memory serves, that when the first E9 promotions were discussed the company had several thousand people and was considering three engineers, each a different archetype. Philip compares this to becoming a professor, where there is no formula and it comes down to whether other E8s think you are an E8.

followups.question: What if an excellent E7 has no E8s or E9s nearby to give qualitative input?
answer: Philip says this happens often at small companies or on weak teams. When Philip worked at Microsoft it had about 140,000 people, and Philip believes it was about 240,000 before the layoffs. In a company that size there are always weak teams, where someone may feel awesome only because peers are weak. That leads to overleveling or to having nobody to learn from. Philip uses a real-estate analogy: you do not want to be the most expensive house on the block, with no room to grow, nor the worst, so find a block where you are the middle house.

At the highest levels, Philip says, good role models are hard to find and each excels differently, so a model may not match your strengths. More useful is a coach who has a say in promotions and can say you are qualitatively far from where you need to be. Then you can discuss what to do about it.
followups.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.question: What project or scope earned Philip the E9 promotion?
answer: Philip brought 12 people to start the engineering portion of Meta's London office and, over roughly four or five years, grew it to about 400 or 500. A good level-six engineering manager could run 12 engineers, Philip says, but with each order of magnitude of growth the problems get harder and the solutions turn gray. The promotion rested on handling a wider variety of things and more strategic decisions.

One example: in one of Philip's last meetings as site lead, Philip argued to people in Menlo Park about how many interns to hire and how much headcount London should have that summer. The argument rested on math about expected H-1B volume 18 months ahead, for full-time offers moving to Menlo Park. Earlier, as an E8, Philip was the first of Meta's sites to look at the seniority pyramid and ask whether people were growing at a commensurate pace. Philip describes these as decisions that grow in scope, by breadth of people affected or by how far ahead one must think.
blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.question: What made the London site's engineering culture strong?
answer: Philip names two helps. First, before London Philip had been the second person hired in Meta Seattle, the company's first office outside its Palo Alto headquarters, and saw it grow from four desks to 120, including mistakes in how it grew. Second, before starting London, Philip interviewed site directors from other companies. One was the former site director of Google London, David Singleton, whom Philip says later became Stripe's CTO.

Singleton told Philip that Google had experimented with landing teams, the group sent to bootstrap a site's culture, and concluded the team should commit for at least two years. Philip contrasts this with companies that send a team for three or six months and then leave the site on its own. Philip thinks that is a mistake, because culture is hard to hold while new people are about as numerous as those who have been around more than three months. The CTO wanted enough engineers for two full interview loops, about 10 to 12 people.

Philip interviewed nearly 50 volunteers from the company, plus some of their peers and their managers, to choose 12 who would carry the culture. Each was asked to bring a project to lead, and the group included exceptional individual contributors who were happy to do whatever the site needed. Philip says Philip was lucky in the choices and credits learning from people who had done it before.

followups.question: Was the two-year commitment tied to pay or a contract?
answer: Philip says no. Pay stayed what it had been and nobody signed anything. Philip had a serious conversation saying Philip wanted only people committed to at least two years, so those who could not commit opted out. One or two had to return sooner for understandable reasons, and Philip supported them.

Far more stayed longer than expected. Philip believes about four of the original team are still in London 15 years later. Philip says they did not join planning to settle there. They loved London and the office.
followups.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.question: Does Philip have favorite stories from working with Zuck and Bos?
answer: Philip's first manager at Facebook was Bos, who later became CTO, and during the London years Philip's manager was the then-CTO captioned as "Shrep." Both gave great advice and guidance. Philip spoke one-on-one with Zuck only a few times, so Philip's insight is limited, but Philip says Zuck felt genuine in how he led.

What impressed Philip most about both Zuck and Bos was their willingness and ability to grow. Philip joined at 33, when the company's median age was 27, and was the oldest person in the Seattle office for the first seven months, so most of the people Philip worked for were younger. People who had worked with either for years could say exactly how they had grown. Philip saw both as open to coaching, probably seeking it, and making a deliberate effort to improve.

Philip's small example is Zuck's AMAs. Within about two years of Philip joining, Philip says, they had improved a lot. Philip is pretty sure someone coached Zuck on how to hold his head, because early on his natural pose had the head tilted slightly upward, and over the years he deliberately corrected it to face the crowd straight on.
blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.question: Which high-profile individual contributor impressed Philip most?
answer: Philip mentions John Carmack, whom Philip calls legendary but worked with only indirectly through Oculus. Beyond being very prolific, Philip says, Carmack could drop into a codebase after about six months away and give concrete advice. On Philip's small product, Oculus 360 Photos, Carmack tried it one day unprompted. He had insights about distortion at the corners of photos while turning and performance ideas that nobody on the team had thought of.

Philip worked more with Scott Renfro, who came to London for a six-month rotation. Peer feedback on him was consistently glowing: even for a dumb mistake, his code review comments were sensitive and never shamed anyone, and peers wrote that he took time out of his day to make them better. Philip calls him a force multiplier for his teams, and says he later led huge infrastructure-wide changes at Meta, with Philip pretty sure GDPR was among them. For Philip he is a clear case of seniority well earned, because he could guarantee a huge scope of work personally and also lift every team he joined.
blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.question: Why did Philip buy the whole company coffee for a day?
answer: The host remembers it as a day of free coffee for everyone and puts the cost at over $23,000. Philip did not state a figure in this answer. Philip says the idea began several years into the Facebook years. After the company moved to its Menlo Park campus, a coffee shop opened in Hacker Square, and one Christmas Philip bought everyone a coffee for a day. Philip found the joy infectious, and the chief executive of the coffee chain wrote to say its staff had never seen anything like it.

When Philip left, Philip wanted to give something back. Philip stresses luck. People forget, Philip says, that when Philip joined, the talk was that Friendster might return, that Google+ would roll over Facebook, and that Facebook would never make money on mobile. Philip had left Microsoft after 12 years, in which Philip says the stock rose about 15 percent, and had low expectations. The Facebook outcome was, in Philip's words, "a brick of money" that came from luck, not design. Philip says Philip gave all IPO proceeds to charity because they felt undeserved, citing luck in being born when an interest in computer science pays and in emigrating to America. Philip then coordinated with coffee shops at the major Facebook sites, around five, by calling the owners, and says it was fun and rewarding.
blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.question: Why did Philip leave Facebook when things were going so well?
answer: Philip says the biggest concern in 2018 was the rising income gap in America. Philip wanted to start a B Corp to bridge it. Philip was already telling co-workers that technical unemployment was coming, before the term was common, because Philip was convinced robots would replace people and society needed to adapt quickly. Most co-workers disagreed. Philip also felt Facebook had grown to where it would be more than fine without Philip.

Judging Philip's own usefulness at the same level as on joining, Philip felt more useful as an individual contributor when Facebook was small. Philip joined as the second person hired in Seattle, when Facebook had about 500 engineers globally. Philip and two other engineers shipped the whole video calling feature in about six months, and Philip also helped negotiate the Skype contract and hire and manage the testing contractors. Eight years later, with thousands of engineers, Philip thought a generalist was much less useful than specialists. Philip felt like a generic coder contributing nothing exceptional.

followups.question: Do small companies generally value generalists more, with specialists favored at the largest companies?
answer: Philip says that is Philip's intuition. Every small company can use at least one specialist in its domain. The bigger force, in Philip's view, is quantization. A large company can hire a full-time communications person, but a small one cannot hire someone for three hours a week, so it asks a product manager who communicates well to cover it for a while.

Generalists can be fractionalized across many roles. Once a company is large enough that each fraction of work needs one or more people full-time, a generalist wastes energy because perhaps 15 percent of their skills apply to the job.
followups.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.question: What brought Philip back into industry, and why OpenAI?
answer: After Facebook, Philip started a local nonprofit in Seattle, captioned "Outere," building free software for global health. A Gates Foundation grant funded it, and Philip says the software was deployed in Nigeria, Kenya and South Africa to assist rapid malaria testing. Philip then took an unemployed break and used GitHub Copilot in VS Code, trying and failing to persuade friends to pay for AI tools.

When AI took off, around the ChatGPT 3.5 or 4 period, Philip saw a huge transition point. Philip felt Philip had missed two while at Microsoft, the dot-com wave and mobile, both of which Microsoft largely missed, and had been lucky to catch the social network wave. Philip increasingly believed AI could be as big as or bigger than the internet. Philip reasons that humans might be the first species to create something smarter than itself, which might even answer the Fermi question.

Philip says Philip applied only to OpenAI because of a Facebook lesson: join the market leader or nobody at all. A leader can afford to fail at a few things and take brave, big shots. A follower such as Google+ has to match all of the leader's checkboxes and add one differentiator, circles in that case, and its timeline is set by the leader. Philip loves the craziness a leader can afford. The plan was to join OpenAI or keep writing software independently.
blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.question: How did OpenAI compare with Facebook?
answer: Philip first notes that the stages differ: Facebook had about 500 engineers when Philip joined and OpenAI about 120. With that caveat, Philip calls OpenAI the highest talent density of any group of engineers Philip has worked with. Moving from Microsoft to Facebook was a big jump in the average quality of colleagues, and Philip felt OpenAI was a notch above that.

followups.question: Was it technical ability that stood out, or something else?
answer: Philip says the technical capabilities were exceptional. The difference Philip names is product focus. Facebook focused heavily on what the product is and why people use it, Philip says, because beyond a network effect and a product people loved it had little magic sauce. In the early ChatGPT days, with no viable competitors, a lousy product could still be used. Philip recalls that a year or two earlier a server error appeared in about every fourth conversation thread.
Philip expects OpenAI to get increasingly better at product. As competition heats up, Philip says, success will come from research shipped in compelling products, not from pure research.
followups.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.question: How did Philip develop such strong writing?
answer: Philip says Philip was a bad writer through college because Philip did not respect communication. Coming from a culture that prized getting A's, Philip viewed the hard sciences as real and history and English as a waste of time, with no right answers, and so did not invest in soft skills.

At Microsoft, in spare time, Philip reread classics hated in high school. Philip names Hemingway and The Great Gatsby, saw them differently as an older reader, and developed a love of language. Philip cites Virginia Woolf for the idea that to write well you need to read well, and names David Foster Wallace, Alice Munro's short stories and Pilgrim at Tinker Creek as writing that shows what language can do. Philip then came to see writing as a skill as valuable as a hard science skill, and started working at it.

Beyond reading well, Philip says, it takes a willingness to rewrite several times and to leave material on the cutting-room floor, and many of Philip's well-known posts were rewritten repeatedly. Philip also notes clever rhetorical moves in other people's Substacks and tries to remember them. Above all, Philip says, the change came from no longer disrespecting the skill and seeing it as essential even for scientists and technical people.

followups.question: Was the non-chronological essay structure planned, and did an editor help?
answer: Philip says the structure came from a moment of inspiration about how to tell that story compellingly. Philip says chronological order is usually the most compelling because it makes sense. Some stories work better out of order, Philip says, because a different, threaded arc in a person's life becomes visible, and Philip felt that way about this one.

Philip had no editor for those pieces. Philip did hire a professional editor, captioned Rebecca Ambrose, for a podcast miniseries, wanting the words well structured and expecting a professional to do better, and learned a great deal. Philip says nothing posted professionally was ever edited by another person, though Philip did receive feedback in the podcast case.
followups.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.question: How did the Great Post Explorer side project come about?
answer: Philip wrote the tool inside Facebook to rank and surface the most commented-on or most reacted-to posts of all time on the company's internal network. Philip had benefited from serendipitously finding great things written by people who came before, and wished they were cataloged and crowdsourced by category so they could be browsed.

Philip's underlying point is that posts fade with time, and in Philip's opinion the value of a post is often temporal, but for some posts it is not, much as some podcasts are evergreen and others cover current news. The tool aimed to help people discover timeless posts. The host recalls it was still live about two years earlier. Philip is not sure what happened to it.
blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.question: Is software engineering like athletics, with a performance peak and then decay?
answer: Philip thinks engineers can keep getting more valuable over time. Everyone's growth curve is asymptotic and everyone has a different final level, so growth slows near it. As with work hours beyond 50 or 60, though, each increment can still be growth, so one need not flatline.

Philip's image is that when young, Philip outran everybody but ran serpentine, and experience means jogging in a straight line. An experienced person senses when things are not heading the right way and either avoids that work or persuades the team to stop early, saving a team's worth of time. Philip's example is a friend at Microsoft whose organization's vice president met weekly to triage bugs for shipping. Philip told the friend that this meant the project was nowhere near shipping on time. Philip says people also learn what is worth investing in.

Philip also values having everyone run in the same direction even if it is three degrees off the ideal. As a young person Philip held the idealistic view that there was one right direction. Philip now thinks a team pulling together at roughly 98 percent correct will get further than half the team pulling perfectly while the other half argues, and links this to Amazon's "disagree and commit." Philip concedes some things decline: Philip lacks the stamina of age 24, and if woken at 3 a.m. today would code slowly, whereas at 23 it was no problem. Philip hopes that while some things weaken, others strengthen.
blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.question: How did Philip win respect as a very young manager?
answer: Philip says it was difficult, because Philip lacked humility and was overly ambitious. Philip says Philip would not have worked for Philip's own 24-year-old self. Philip became a manager because Philip was one of the team's strongest engineers, and the team figured it was better to keep a good engineer happy by letting Philip manage.

In that first year, at 24, Philip had to fire a 40-year-old. Philip calls it exceptionally difficult, made harder by awareness of how junior Philip was. Philip says the person deserved it for missing expectations but was two levels above Philip's own level, and Philip says Philip was too immature to know how to manage someone more experienced.

Philip says Philip was a pretty bad manager at first but obsessed with growth: Philip collected mentors, asked for feedback and read nonfiction about managing teams and hard conversations. Philip says Philip made huge mistakes even in the last year of managing. The biggest weakness Philip names is giving feedback. Philip pulls punches, hates confrontation and downplays how serious the feedback is, so people miss the point. Philip says Philip has gone from very bad to passable and does not expect to become excellent. A strength is motivating action, since Philip joins only teams Philip believes in, and Philip's passion and vision excite people.
blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.question: Should someone early in their career become a specialist or a generalist?
answer: Philip calls this tricky and dependent on how well a person knows themselves. A chess prodigy who is clearly gifted by eight or nine should specialize. Most people lack that certainty, and Philip would caution against binding too early to a specialty.

Philip names three dangers. First, how can you know you are a specialist rather than a generalist without having been a generalist? Second, an idiot-savant risk. Philip's example is the mathematician Erdős, who Philip says did not know as an adult how to cut his own grapefruit, so his mother cut it, although he published a great deal. Third, the specialty may disappear, especially in the age of AI. Philip compares a specialist in a fading technology to a COBOL expert hoping for another Y2K. Philip would encourage someone starting at 22 or 23 to dabble in a few things before committing hard.
blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.question: If Philip could advise a younger self at the start of the career, what would the advice be?
answer: Philip first cites Roy Disney, that decisions are easy when your values are clear. Philip's decisions were often hard because Philip lacked clear values, so Philip would tell a younger self to spend more time on what Philip actually wanted before committing.

Philip also says Philip was "the dog that caught the car." On joining Microsoft, Philip was convinced the goal was dev manager, and for about eight years took any job that moved closer, which made decisions easy. When Philip reached the level, which Philip places at around age 30 though the captions are unclear, and saw that E7 might be a terminal level, Philip had no mental model for what came next. Philip likens it to a child actor who peaked early and faces decades of work. Philip says this led to a period of serious depression after losing a sense of purpose. The second caution is to be sure you want what you want: people love Warren Buffett's billions, Philip says, but would they want them in their late 90s?

Philip adds that some things bend and some break. While Philip kept sleeping bags in the office, a fiancee visited from Maryland, and Philip saw her only each evening at 11 p.m., when work ended, for a late Denny's dinner. Philip says Philip is lucky that she is now Philip's wife, and says listeners usually guess the story ends with the engagement ring being returned. Philip recognizes now that Philip was bending something to an extreme that most things would not survive.

For anyone who cares only about career and wants the fastest route, Philip says first be sure that is what you want, and then be sure you are comfortable with other things breaking. Philip would tell the younger self that reaching E7 at 30 rather than 38 makes no difference in the long arc, since there are still about 30 years of work after 38. The real question, Philip says, is how fast you want to reach a terminal level versus keeping healthy relationships with a spouse and children.

followups.question: Would the younger Philip have accepted that advice?
answer: Philip says no. Advice feels good to give, but Philip says about 90 percent of the time you have to be ready to receive it for it to matter, and Philip was nowhere near that level of maturity. Philip compares it to being told that money does not buy happiness: everybody thinks they are the exception, but an unhappy person is still unhappy ten years later with more to spend.
followups.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.question: Is there a closing idea Philip wants the audience to consider?
answer: Philip says Philip remains concerned about technical unemployment. Philip says the change from technology will be massive and will come sooner than people expect. Philip thinks Americans need to work out how to help the average person through it, and that very bad things can happen if society is not helped to adapt. Philip links this to Philip's earlier worries about automation and the rising income gap.
blocks.speaker: Philip Su
